proposals.before: Book of Sui, 54th year of Volume, 19th year of Biography
proposals.after: Book of Sui, Volume 54, Biography 19
proposals.reason: 卷五十四列傳第十九 means 'Volume 54, Biography (liezhuan) 19'. The idiomatic rendering garbles the volume/biography numbering into spurious ordinal 'years' ('54th year of Volume, 19th year of Biography'), misparsing 卷 and 列傳 as if they were reign-year counters rather than the volume and biography numbers of the compilation.

proposals.before: His grandfather Pi had been Wei’s grand preceptor.
proposals.after: His grandfather Pi had been Wei's Grand Commandant.
proposals.reason: 太尉 is the office of Grand Commandant, one of the Three Ducal Ministers (with Chancellor and Minister of Works); it is a distinct office from 太師 Grand Preceptor (held elsewhere in this chapter by Li Yan's father Bi, s0033, correctly rendered). The idiomatic translation conflates the two offices.

proposals.before: His grandfather Pi was Grand Preceptor of Wei.
proposals.after: His grandfather Pi was Grand Commandant of Wei.
proposals.reason: Same error as the idiomatic rendering of this unit: 太尉 (Grand Commandant) is mistranslated as 'Grand Preceptor', the title proper to the distinct office 太師.

proposals.before: Changshu had dignified bearing even as a child. At eight, Emperor Wu of Zhou saw him and marveled, saying, "Duke Wang has this grandson—that alone is enough to make his line immortal."
proposals.after: Changshu had dignified bearing even as a child. At eight, Zhou Taizu saw him and marveled, saying, "Duke Wang has this grandson—that alone is enough to make his line immortal."
proposals.reason: 周太祖 (Zhou Taizu, i.e. Yuwen Tai, the pre-dynastic Western Wei regent, d. AD 556) is mistranslated here as 'Emperor Wu of Zhou'. Emperor Wu (武帝, Yuwen Yong, r. AD 561-578) is a different, later ruler who is correctly named elsewhere in this chapter (e.g. s0062, s0098). Changshu's childhood encounter necessarily predates the Zhou founding in AD 557 and so can only be with Taizu.

proposals.before: From childhood Changshu had dignified bearing. At eight years of age, Emperor Wu of Zhou saw him and was struck by him, saying: "The Duke Wang has this grandson; that is enough for immortality."
proposals.after: From childhood Changshu had dignified bearing. At eight years of age, Zhou Taizu saw him and was struck by him, saying: "The Duke Wang has this grandson; that is enough for immortality."
proposals.reason: Same 周太祖/Zhou Taizu vs. Emperor Wu confusion as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: Under Emperor Wu of Zhou he entered service as a thousand-ox guard attendant and was enfeoffed as duke of Huairen county.
proposals.after: Under Zhou Taizu he entered service as a thousand-ox guard attendant and was enfeoffed as duke of Huairen county.
proposals.reason: 周太祖 (Zhou Taizu / Yuwen Tai) is again mistranslated as 'Emperor Wu of Zhou' (see s0006). Li Yan's entry into service, prior to the offices he holds later under the Zhou dynasty proper (s0036 onward), dates to the Western Wei/pre-dynastic period associated with Taizu, not the later reign of Emperor Wu (AD 561-578).

proposals.before: In the time of Emperor Wu of Zhou, he left commoner status as Thousand-Ox Guard Attendant and was enfeoffed as Duke of Huairen County.
proposals.after: In the time of Zhou Taizu, he left commoner status as Thousand-Ox Guard Attendant and was enfeoffed as Duke of Huairen County.
proposals.reason: Same 周太祖/Zhou Taizu vs. Emperor Wu confusion as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: first year of In of Kaihuang, again as campaign commander, he suppressed rebellious tribes and pacified them.
proposals.after: In the first year of Kaihuang, again as campaign commander, he suppressed rebellious tribes and pacified them.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic rendering garbles 開皇元年 ('the first year of Kaihuang') into the malformed phrase 'first year of In of Kaihuang', apparently a corrupted template substitution for 'In the Nth year of X'. The literal translation of the same unit already has the correct phrasing ('In the first year of Kaihuang').

proposals.before: He followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuwen Jiong at Xiangzhou and was made pillar of the state.
proposals.after: He followed Wei Xiaokuan in defeating Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou and was made pillar of the state.
proposals.reason: 尉遲迥 romanizes as Yuchi Jiong (surname 尉遲, Yuchi). The translation wrongly substitutes the surname Yuwen (宇文, the Zhou imperial clan name), producing a fictitious name. This is the historical general Yuchi Jiong, whose rebellion against Emperor Wen at Xiangzhou in AD 580 is a well-documented event.

proposals.before: Following Wei Xiaokuan, he defeated Yuwen Jiong at Xiangzhou and was appointed Pillar of the State.
proposals.after: Following Wei Xiaokuan, he defeated Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou and was appointed Pillar of the State.
proposals.reason: Same 尉遲迥/Yuchi Jiong vs. Yuwen Jiong error as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: Grand preceptor Yuwen Hu brought him in as clerk of central and external military affairs.
proposals.after: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu brought him in as clerk of central and external military affairs.
proposals.reason: 大塚宰 (head of the Zhou dynasty's Six Ministries, modeled on the Rites of Zhou) is rendered in this corpus's house style as 'Grand Steward of the Tomb' (a literal calque on 塚, 'mound/tomb', kept consistent across chapters for this office). This unit instead uses 'Grand preceptor', which duplicates the distinct office 太師 and breaks that consistency; Yuwen Hu held 大塚宰, not 太師.

proposals.before: Grand Preceptor Yuwen Hu recruited him as Clerk of Central and External Military Affairs.
proposals.after: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu recruited him as Clerk of Central and External Military Affairs.
proposals.reason: Same 大塚宰 house-style inconsistency as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: His father Jihai had been Wei's minister of education and king of Fenyang; when Zhou and Qi split the realm, Jihai entered service in Chang'an.
proposals.after: His father Jihai had been Wei's minister of education and king of Fengyi; when Zhou and Qi split the realm, Jihai entered service in Chang'an.
proposals.reason: 馮翊 (Fengyi commandery, near Chang'an, historically "Left Fengyi" 左馮翊) is mistranslated as "Fenyang" (汾陽, an unrelated place in Shanxi, famous later as Guo Ziyi's Tang-era title). The same substitution recurs at s0124 for Heng's own inherited title.

proposals.before: His father Jihai was Minister of Education and King of Fenyang under Wei; when Zhou and Qi were divided, Jihai took office in Chang'an.
proposals.after: His father Jihai was Minister of Education and King of Fengyi under Wei; when Zhou and Qi were divided, Jihai took office in Chang'an.
proposals.reason: Same 馮翊/Fengyi vs. Fenyang substitution as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou was delighted to see them and, because Heng was the son of a founding minister, treated him with exceptional favor.
proposals.after: Zhou Taizu was delighted to see them and, because Heng was the son of a founding minister, treated him with exceptional favor.
proposals.reason: 周太祖 (Zhou Taizu, i.e. Yuwen Tai, the pre-dynastic Western Wei regent, d. AD 556) is mistranslated as "Emperor Wu of Zhou". Emperor Wu (Yuwen Yong, r. AD 561-578) is a different, later ruler correctly named elsewhere in this chapter (e.g. s0128, s0148 context). Heng's arrival in Chang'an as a child necessarily predates the Zhou founding in AD 557 and Emperor Wu's reign.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou saw them and was greatly pleased; because Heng was the son of a founding minister, he treated him with exceptional courtesy.
proposals.after: Zhou Taizu saw them and was greatly pleased; because Heng was the son of a founding minister, he treated him with exceptional courtesy.
proposals.reason: Same 周太祖/Zhou Taizu vs. Emperor Wu confusion as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou brought him in as a trusted intimate.
proposals.after: Zhou Taizu brought him in as a trusted intimate.
proposals.reason: 周太祖 (Zhou Taizu, Yuwen Tai) is again mistranslated as "Emperor Wu of Zhou" (see s0121). Du Zheng inherited his marquisate at the end of the Wei Datong era (s0147, circa AD 551) and was recruited immediately afterward, i.e. under the pre-dynastic regent Taizu, not the later Emperor Wu (r. AD 561-578).

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou recruited him as a trusted intimate.
proposals.after: Zhou Taizu recruited him as a trusted intimate.
proposals.reason: Same 周太祖/Zhou Taizu vs. Emperor Wu confusion as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: When Emperor Wen was chancellor, Yuwen Jiong rebelled; Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and other men of Luoyang raised troops in support of him.
proposals.after: When Emperor Wen was chancellor, Yuchi Jiong rebelled; Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and other men of Luoyang raised troops in support of him.
proposals.reason: 尉遲迥 romanizes as Yuchi Jiong (surname 尉遲, Yuchi). The translation wrongly substitutes the surname Yuwen (宇文, the Zhou imperial clan name), producing a fictitious name. This is the historical general Yuchi Jiong, whose rebellion against Emperor Wen at Xiangzhou in AD 580 is well documented (cf. s0101 in this chapter's Tian Rengong biography, which has the identical error).

proposals.before: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, Yuwen Jiong rebelled; the men of Luoyang Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and others raised troops in response to Jiong.
proposals.after: When Emperor Wen became Chancellor, Yuchi Jiong rebelled; the men of Luoyang Liang Kang, Xing Liushui, and others raised troops in response to Jiong.
proposals.reason: Same 尉遲迥/Yuchi Jiong vs. Yuwen Jiong error as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: Grand preceptor Yuwen Hu brought him in as a trusted intimate; he was soon made palace attendant major and rose to commandant of the imperial carriages.
proposals.after: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu brought him in as a trusted intimate; he was soon made palace attendant major and rose to commandant of the imperial carriages.
proposals.reason: 大塚宰 (head of the Zhou dynasty's Six Ministries, modeled on the Rites of Zhou) is rendered in this corpus's house style as 'Grand Steward of the Tomb' (cf. part-a s0095, same office held by the same man, Yuwen Hu). This unit instead uses 'Grand preceptor', duplicating the distinct office 太師 and breaking that consistency.

proposals.before: Grand Preceptor Yuwen Hu recruited him as a trusted intimate; soon he was appointed Palace Attendant Major and was promoted in succession to Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.
proposals.after: Grand Steward of the Tomb Yuwen Hu recruited him as a trusted intimate; soon he was appointed Palace Attendant Major and was promoted in succession to Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.
proposals.reason: Same 大塚宰 house-style inconsistency as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: sixth year of In of Kaihuang, when the Turks raided the frontier, Prince Wei Shuang was ordered to command the northern campaign and Zheng was made campaign commander and chief of staff to the supreme commander.
proposals.after: In the sixth year of Kaihuang, when the Turks raided the frontier, Prince Wei Shuang was ordered to command the northern campaign and Zheng was made campaign commander and chief of staff to the supreme commander.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic rendering garbles 開皇六年 ('the sixth year of Kaihuang', AD 586) into the malformed phrase 'sixth year of In of Kaihuang', the same corrupted template substitution for 'In the Nth year of X' seen at s0042 in part-a. The literal translation of the same unit already has the correct phrasing.

proposals.before: Che was by nature resolute and firm, had capacity and ability, possessed a imposing appearance, and was skilled in many martial arts.
proposals.after: Che was by nature resolute and firm, had capacity and ability, possessed an imposing appearance, and was skilled in many martial arts.
proposals.reason: Grammatical error: the indefinite article 'a' should be 'an' before the vowel-initial word 'imposing' ('a imposing appearance' -> 'an imposing appearance'). The idiomatic rendering of the same unit does not have this error.

proposals.before: He again followed the emperor in defeating Qi forces north of the Fen River, pressed the victory to take Gaobi and Jinyang, and helped capture Gao Huan at Jizhou.
proposals.after: He again followed the emperor in defeating Qi forces north of the Fen River, pressed the victory to take Gaobi and Jinyang, and helped capture Gao Jie at Jizhou.
proposals.reason: 髙湝 (Gao Jie), the tenth son of Gao Huan and Prince of Rencheng, is mistranslated as "Gao Huan" -- his own father, Emperor Shenwu of Qi (d. AD 547), who had died three decades before this AD 577 campaign. Gao Jie made a last stand at Xindu/Jizhou and was captured by Yuwen Xian's forces per external sources (Bei Qi Shu juan 12).

proposals.before: Again he followed the Emperor in defeating Qi forces north of the Fen River, pressed the victory to take Gaobi, captured Jinyang, and at Jizhou seized Gao Huan—all with notable contribution.
proposals.after: Again he followed the Emperor in defeating Qi forces north of the Fen River, pressed the victory to take Gaobi, captured Jinyang, and at Jizhou seized Gao Jie—all with notable contribution.
proposals.reason: Same 髙湝/Gao Jie vs. Gao Huan error as in the idiomatic rendering of this unit; see rationale there.

proposals.before: tenth year of In of Kaihuang he was raised to pillar of the state.
proposals.after: In the tenth year of Kaihuang he was raised to pillar of the state.
proposals.reason: Same malformed 'Nth year of In of X' template substitution for 開皇十年 ('the tenth year of Kaihuang', AD 590) as seen at s0156 in the Du Zheng biography; the literal rendering of the same unit already has the correct phrasing.

proposals.before: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, Peng was made grand general of the left forward command.
proposals.after: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, Peng was transferred to grand general of the Left Leading Army.
proposals.reason: 遷 means transfer/promotion to an office, not merely being made; 左領軍 is the Left Leading Army (a Guard command), not a 'forward command'.

proposals.before: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, Peng was transferred to Grand General of the Left Forward Command.
proposals.after: When Emperor Yang ascended the throne, Peng was transferred to Grand General of the Left Leading Army.
proposals.reason: 左領軍 denotes the Left Leading Army office; 'Forward Command' misreads 領軍.

proposals.before: With Prince of Han Liang just pacified and remnant factions gathering, the emperor ordered Peng to lead tens of thousands of men to suppress the east of the mountains and again to hold charge of Cizhou.
proposals.after: With Liang, the Prince of Han, just pacified and remnant factions gathering, the emperor ordered Peng to lead tens of thousands of men to suppress the east of the mountains and again to hold charge of Cizhou.
proposals.reason: 漢王諒 is Liang, Prince of Han; 'Prince of Han Liang' fuses the fief title Han with the personal name Liang.

proposals.before: At the time Prince of Han Liang had just been pacified and remnant factions were often gathering; the Emperor ordered Peng to lead several tens of thousands of men to suppress the east of the mountains and again to hold charge of Cizhou affairs.
proposals.after: At the time Liang, the Prince of Han, had just been pacified and remnant factions were often gathering; the Emperor ordered Peng to lead several tens of thousands of men to suppress the east of the mountains and again to hold charge of Cizhou affairs.
proposals.reason: 漢王諒 is Liang, Prince of Han; 'Prince of Han Liang' reverses and fuses title and given name.

decisions.reason: s0001 reads 隋書卷五十四列傳第十九; 卷 and 列傳 mark volume and biography numbers, so “54th year of Volume / 19th year of Biography” invents reign-year counters the Chinese does not have, and the proposed wording matches the source.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 隋書卷五十四列傳第十九

decisions.reason: s0004 has 魏太尉; 太尉 is Grand Commandant, distinct from 太師 Grand Preceptor, so the idiomatic “grand preceptor” is a wrong office and the proposed Grand Commandant is accurate.
The same 太尉 in s0004 must be Grand Commandant in the literal field; “Grand Preceptor” is the English for 太師, not for this office.
s0006 has 周太祖見而異之; 周太祖 is Zhou Taizu (Yuwen Tai), not Emperor Wu (武帝), so the idiomatic substitution invents the wrong ruler.
The same 周太祖 in s0006 requires Zhou Taizu in the literal field; “Emperor Wu of Zhou” misidentifies the person named in the Chinese.
s0035 opens 周太祖時; that is the time of Zhou Taizu, not of Emperor Wu, so the idiomatic “Under Emperor Wu of Zhou” is a factual misidentification.
Literal “In the time of Emperor Wu of Zhou” likewise contradicts s0035’s 周太祖時; Zhou Taizu is the correct referent.
s0042 begins 開皇元年, “the first year of Kaihuang”; the garbled “first year of In of Kaihuang” is not English supported by the Chinese, and the proposed phrasing restores the date formula.
s0101 has 破尉遲迥于相州; 尉遲 is the surname Yuchi, not Yuwen, so “Yuwen Jiong” invents a false name and Yuchi Jiong is correct.
The same 尉遲迥 in s0101 must be Yuchi Jiong in the literal field; “Yuwen Jiong” wrongly substitutes the Zhou imperial surname.
s0095 has 大塚宰宇文護; 大塚宰 is not 太師, so “Grand preceptor” is the wrong office, and the proposed house-style “Grand Steward of the Tomb” correctly distinguishes that Zhou office.
Literal “Grand Preceptor” for the same 大塚宰 in s0095 likewise conflates it with 太師; the proposed title restores the correct office reading.
s0115 has 馮翊王; 馮翊 is Fengyi, not Fenyang (汾陽), so “king of Fenyang” misplaces the title and Fengyi is the accurate reading.
The same 馮翊王 in s0115 requires King of Fengyi in the literal field; “Fenyang” is an unrelated toponym.
s0121 has 周太祖見而大悅; again 周太祖 is Zhou Taizu, not Emperor Wu, so the idiomatic ruler name is wrong.
Literal “Emperor Wu of Zhou” for s0121’s 周太祖 is the same misidentification; Zhou Taizu matches the Chinese.
s0148 reads 周太祖引為親信; the agent is Zhou Taizu, so “Emperor Wu of Zhou” invents the wrong patron.
The same 周太祖 in s0148 must be Zhou Taizu in the literal field; Emperor Wu is unsupported by this sentence.
s0130 has 遇尉遲迥作亂; 尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not Yuwen Jiong, so the idiomatic surname error invents a false rebel.
Literal “Yuwen Jiong” for the same 尉遲迥 in s0130 is likewise wrong; Yuchi Jiong is the name the Chinese gives.
s0169 has 大塚宰宇文護; as at s0095, “Grand preceptor” misreads that office as 太師, and the proposed title correctly names 大塚宰.
Literal “Grand Preceptor” for s0169’s 大塚宰 is the same office error; the proposed wording restores the distinct Zhou title.
s0156 begins 開皇六年; “sixth year of In of Kaihuang” is a corrupted date template, and “In the sixth year of Kaihuang” restores the Chinese era-year formula.
The literal field’s “a imposing appearance” is ungrammatical English before a vowel sound; changing the article to “an” fixes a real error without altering meaning.
s0179 has 擒髙湝於冀州; 髙湝 is Gao Jie, not Gao Huan, so the idiomatic capture of Gao Huan invents the wrong captive.
Literal “seized Gao Huan” for the same 髙湝 is likewise wrong; Gao Jie matches the personal name in the Chinese.
s0204 reads 開皇十年; “tenth year of In of Kaihuang” is the same broken date template, and the proposed phrasing correctly renders the era year.
s0249 has 遷左領軍大將軍; 遷 is transfer to office and 左領軍 is the Left Leading Army, so “made … left forward command” both softens 遷 and misnames 領軍.
Literal “Left Forward Command” misreads 左領軍; Left Leading Army is the correct office name for this Guard command.
s0251 has 漢王諒; that is Liang, Prince of Han, and “Prince of Han Liang” fuses title and given name into an ambiguous English form the proposed wording clarifies.
The same 漢王諒 in s0251 should be “Liang, the Prince of Han” in the literal field; “Prince of Han Liang” reverses and blends title with the personal name.
